title: (Scenario) A Playwright suite passes locally but fails in Jenkins/CI — how do you debug it by finding the ENVIRONMENTAL difference (Node/Playwright/browser versions, env vars, OS, test data, network access, authentication, time zones, file paths, available CPU/memory) and inspecting CI logs, screenshots, videos, and traces — and why reproduce the difference instead of randomly editing the test?
shortTitle: (Scenario) A Playwright suite passes locally but fails in CI

s1_definition.profdef: When a Playwright suite passes locally but fails in CI, the failure is almost always an environmental difference, not a test-logic bug, so the debugging method is to systematically compare the two environments and inspect the CI diagnostics. The dimensions to check are Node, Playwright, and browser versions, environment variables, operating system, test data, network access and firewalls, authentication, time zones and locale, file paths, and available CPU and memory, using the CI logs, screenshots, videos, and traces to see what actually happened. You reproduce the environmental difference rather than randomly editing the test because a change that happens to make CI green without understanding the cause usually breaks something else or hides the real problem.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India tests run perfectly on your own desk but fail on the shared night-shift machine. Randomly changing the tests until the night machine goes green is like adjusting your car's engine until a warning light turns off without knowing why it was on, you might just disconnect the warning. The right approach is to compare the two machines carefully: do they run the same browser version, the same settings, the same time zone, can the night machine even reach the staging server, does it have the login secret, does it have enough memory. Then you look at the night machine's own evidence, its logs and the screenshots, videos, and traces it recorded, to see exactly what went wrong. Once you find the real difference, you fix that, and the test becomes reliable everywhere instead of accidentally patched.

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** When a Playwright suite passes locally but fails in CI, the failure is almost always an environmental difference, not a test-logic bug, so the debugging method is to systematically compare the two environments and inspect the CI diagnostics. The dimensions to check are Node, Playwright, and browser versions, environment variables, operating system, test data, network access and firewalls, authentication, time zones and locale, file paths, and available CPU and memory, using the CI logs, screenshots, videos, and traces to see what actually happened. You reproduce the environmental difference rather than randomly editing the test because a change that happens to make CI green without understanding the cause usually breaks something else or hides the real problem.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India tests run perfectly on your own desk but fail on the shared night-shift machine. Randomly changing the tests until the night machine goes green is like adjusting your car's engine until a warning light turns off without knowing why it was on, you might just disconnect the warning. The right approach is to compare the two machines carefully: do they run the same browser version, the same settings, the same time zone, can the night machine even reach the staging server, does it have the login secret, does it have enough memory. Then you look at the night machine's own evidence, its logs and the screenshots, videos, and traces it recorded, to see exactly what went wrong. Once you find the real difference, you fix that, and the test becomes reliable everywhere instead of accidentally patched.

**One line to remember:** A pass-locally-fail-in-CI suite is an environmental difference, so compare versions, env vars, OS, data, network, auth, time zone, paths, and resources and read the CI traces, videos, and screenshots, and fix the real difference rather than randomly editing the test, which only hides the cause.

sections.s2_technical:
The key insight is that identical test code behaving differently in two places means the environments differ, so debugging is a comparison exercise, not a guess-and-edit exercise. You start by gathering the CI evidence, because Playwright is designed to produce it: the CI logs show the command, the environment, and the error; the on-failure screenshot shows the visual state; the video shows the sequence; and the trace, opened in the trace viewer, shows the timeline with DOM snapshots, network requests and responses, and console logs, which usually reveals the failure's nature, an element never appeared, a request returned an error, the page was on a login screen, and so on. This evidence narrows which environmental dimension to investigate.

Then you compare the dimensions one by one. Node, Playwright, and browser versions differing between local and CI can change behavior or available APIs, so you pin versions, local and CI should install from the same lockfile and the same Playwright version, which also controls the browser binaries. Environment variables differing is extremely common: a base URL, a feature flag, or a timeout set locally but missing or different in CI changes what the test hits; you diff the variables. Operating system differences, often macOS or Windows locally versus Linux in CI, affect fonts, rendering, default browser behavior, and especially file paths, so you account for the Linux runner. Test data differences matter when local uses a seeded database and CI points at a shared or empty environment, so the data the test assumes may be absent; you ensure data is created by the test. Network access is a frequent culprit: the CI runner may sit behind a firewall that blocks the application, a third-party service, or a CDN, so a request silently fails; you check connectivity and consider mocking external calls. Authentication differs when local reuses a logged-in session or a locally stored secret that CI lacks, so the test lands on a login page; you confirm the secret is injected in CI. Time zone and locale differences cause date, time, and currency assertions to fail, because the Linux runner may be in UTC while your laptop is in local time; you set a fixed time zone and locale or write tz-aware assertions. File paths break when tests use absolute or OS-specific paths that do not exist on the runner; you use relative, OS-agnostic paths. And available CPU and memory are lower or more contended in CI, so tests that are timing-sensitive or run with too many workers time out under load; you right-size parallelism and timeouts for the runner.

The reason to reproduce the difference rather than randomly edit the test is correctness and durability. Randomly adding a sleep, loosening an assertion, or adding a retry until CI turns green treats the symptom without understanding the cause, and that has three bad outcomes: it often hides a real defect, for example a genuine timing or data problem that also affects users; it is fragile, because the accidental fix frequently breaks under slightly different conditions or masks the next failure; and it degrades the test, loosening assertions reduces the coverage that gave the test value. Reproducing the difference, ideally by running the suite in a container or environment that matches CI, Linux, the same versions, the same variables, the same time zone, lets you see the failure locally, identify the true cause, and fix that cause, which makes the test pass reliably in both places and often fixes a class of latent issues. The senior nuances are to make environments as identical as possible to prevent the problem, pin versions via lockfiles and the Playwright version, run CI in a reproducible container you can also run locally, inject all required variables and secrets, fix time zone and locale explicitly, and treat a local-pass-CI-fail as a signal to understand an environmental gap rather than to tamper with the test. This discipline is what separates genuinely fixing a flaky-across-environments test from accidentally silencing it.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India transfer suite passes on a developer's Mac but fails in the Linux CI because the runner is in UTC while the laptop is in India time, so a date assertion mismatches. The fix is to find and set the time zone, not to loosen the assertion. This is exactly the time-zone dimension.

Problem 2 — Another failure is because the CI runner lacks the injected test password, so tests land on the login page. The fix is to inject the secret, not to skip the login. This is exactly the authentication dimension.

Problem 3 — A third is because CI points at an empty environment where the assumed account does not exist. The fix is to create data in the test. This is exactly the test-data dimension.

In the mini-project we build an environment-comparison tool that captures the key dimensions for two environments, diffs them, and pinpoints the differences that would cause failures, modeling the disciplined compare-and-reproduce approach. We write a Java harness.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/qa/cidebug/*.java

# Run
java -cp out com.bank.qa.cidebug.CiDebugDemo

# Reproduce CI locally (the disciplined approach): run in a matching container
docker run --rm -it -e TZ=UTC -e BASE_URL=https://staging.nationalbank.example \
  -v "$PWD":/work -w /work mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.47.0-jammy \
  bash -lc 'npm ci && npx playwright test'
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two environment snapshots, a local one where the suite passes and a CI one where it fails, each recording the key dimensions.

Step 1: The differ compares the two snapshots dimension by dimension. The Node and Playwright versions match, so those are ruled out, demonstrating that comparison eliminates suspects as well as finding them.

Step 2: It flags the operating-system difference, macOS locally versus Linux in CI, which can affect fonts, rendering, and file paths, and notes that as a possible cause to keep in mind.

Step 3: It flags the time-zone difference, India time locally versus UTC in CI, with the hint that date, time, and currency assertions will mismatch, which is a classic local-pass-CI-fail cause.

Step 4: It flags the missing test password in CI, with the hint that authentication will fail and tests will land on the login page, and the base-URL difference pointing CI at a staging environment where the assumed data may be absent, plus restricted network access and fewer CPU cores.

Step 5: The demo lists the real differences and prescribes fixing the environmental causes, injecting the secret, pinning the time zone, allowing network, sizing workers, rather than editing the test, and shows reproducing the failure locally by running in a Linux container matched to CI, which is the disciplined route to a durable fix.

Final output:

```

2026-10-30 09:52:40 [WARNING] DIFF cpuCores: LOCAL=10  CI=2  -> likely cause: fewer cores -> oversubscribed workers time out
2026-10-30 09:52:40 [WARNING] DIFF networkAccess: LOCAL=full  CI=restricted  -> likely cause: firewall blocks app/3rd-party -> request fails
2026-10-30 09:52:40 [WARNING] DIFF os: LOCAL=macOS  CI=Linux  -> likely cause: fonts/rendering/file paths differ
2026-10-30 09:52:40 [WARNING] DIFF timeZone: LOCAL=Asia/Kolkata  CI=UTC  -> likely cause: date/time/currency assertions mismatch
```

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Suite: PASS local / FAIL CI
    │
    ▼
  Gather CI evidence: logs + screenshot + video + TRACE (what happened)
    │
    ▼
  Compare environments dimension by dimension:
    node/playwright/browser versions | env vars | OS | test data
    network access | auth/secrets | time zone/locale | file paths | CPU/mem
    │
    ▼
  Identify the REAL difference (e.g. UTC vs IST, missing secret)
    │
    ▼
  Reproduce by MATCHING CI locally (Linux container, same vars/tz)
    │
    ▼
  Fix the ENVIRONMENTAL cause (not the test) → passes everywhere
    │  (random test edits → hide defect / fragile / lose coverage)
    ▼
  Prevent: pin versions, container parity, inject vars, fix tz
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
When a Playwright suite passes locally but fails in CI, I start from the principle that identical test code behaving differently in two places means the environments differ, so this is a comparison exercise, not a guess-and-edit exercise. First I gather the CI evidence, because Playwright produces it: the CI logs, the on-failure screenshot, the video, and above all the trace, which in the trace viewer shows the timeline with DOM snapshots, the network requests and responses, and the console logs, and usually reveals the nature of the failure, an element never appeared, a request errored, the page was on a login screen. That narrows which dimension to check. Then I compare the environments dimension by dimension: Node, Playwright, and browser versions, which I pin via the lockfile and the Playwright version so local and CI match; environment variables, which commonly differ, a base URL or feature flag set locally but missing in CI; the operating system, usually macOS or Windows locally versus Linux in CI, which affects fonts, rendering, and file paths; test data, since CI may point at a shared or empty environment where the assumed account does not exist; network access, since the runner may sit behind a firewall that blocks the app or a third party; authentication, since local may reuse a session or secret that CI lacks, landing on a login page; time zone and locale, since the runner is often UTC while my laptop is local time, breaking date and currency assertions; file paths, which must be relative and OS-agnostic; and available CPU and memory, which are lower in CI so timing-sensitive tests or too many workers time out.

The reason I reproduce the difference rather than randomly edit the test is correctness and durability. Adding a sleep, loosening an assertion, or adding a retry until CI goes green treats the symptom without understanding the cause, and that hides real defects, is fragile because it breaks under slightly different conditions, and loosening assertions destroys the coverage that made the test valuable. Instead I reproduce the failure locally by matching CI, running the suite in a Linux container with the same versions, variables, and time zone, so I can see the failure, find the true cause, and fix that, which makes the test reliable in both places and often fixes a class of latent issues.

At the National Bank of India exactly this happened: a transfer suite passed on a developer's Mac but failed in Linux CI. The trace showed a date assertion mismatch, and comparing environments revealed the runner was UTC while the laptop was India time; separately the CI runner was missing the injected test password. I fixed the real causes, pinning the time zone and writing tz-aware assertions and injecting the secret, rather than loosening the test, and ran it in a Playwright container matching CI to confirm. It then passed everywhere. Being able to name the environmental dimensions, use the CI trace and video to localize the failure, and insist on reproducing and fixing the real difference rather than tampering with the test is what shows an interviewer I debug cross-environment failures like an engineer rather than chasing a green checkmark.
